name: Abandoning the Dharma (chos spong ba)
description: The grave fault of disparaging or rejecting any authentic teaching of the Buddha; the Rimé masters apply it to sectarian disparagement of other traditions.
notes: The fault is a general Mahāyāna category (saddharma-pratikṣepa); its Rimé application is recalled, the specific passage is not.

name: The conceit of identity with God
description: The thought 'I am Brahman / I am ever the Lord, and the world is unreal', which the texts attribute to the asuras and describe as leading to blinding darkness; it contradicts experience and scripture.
notes: Recorded as the tradition states it (polemical).

name: Covetousness and displeasure (abhijjhādomanassa)
description: What the monk puts away with regard to the world in each of the four contemplations (MN 10:3); the refrain describes clinging to nothing in the world (mn10:5).

name: Pride of the gods
description: The gods, taking brahman's victory for their own, grew proud; they could not recognize the yakṣa until Umā revealed that it was brahman (Kena 3.1-4.1).
antidotes: knowledge that the victory is brahman's (Kena 4.1)

name: Pride and hypocrisy (abhimāna, dambha)
description: The Lord dislikes pride and loves humility (NBS 27); pride, hypocrisy and the like are to be abandoned (NBS 64); pride of learning and birth has no place among devotees (NBS 72).

name: Clinging to life (abhiniveśa)
description: Flowing by its own momentum, rooted thus even in the learned (YS 2.9). Vyāsa: in every living being there is the constant wish 'may I not cease to be; may I be'; even a worm just born shows fear of death, of the nature of the view of annihilation; both the deluded and the wise have this tendency (vāsanā) from the experience of the pain of death (YBh 2.9).

name: Birth in Mūla
description: Birth in the asterism Mūla, especially its first part, held harmful to the father; pacified by the Mūla-śānti (BPHS 93).

name: Adharma / sin (pāpa)
description: Demerit produced by prohibited acts; with dharma it produces embodiment and must be exhausted for release.
alt_description: The second impurity; destroyed by the observance and by the transfer of demerit to revilers.

name: Adharma as the root of epidemics
description: Unrighteous rule and conduct drive away the gods and disturb seasons, water, land and herbs, so that many fall ill at once (Ca Vi 3.20-23).
antidotes: truth, compassion, giving, worship, good conduct, continence, company of the righteous (Vi 3.15-17)

name: The adventitious stains (glo bur gyi dri ma)
description: The conventional obscurations covering buddha-nature, which are other than it and separable from it; removing them uncovers qualities that were always present.
antidotes: hearing, reflection and meditation on the definitive meaning

name: Disorders of the digestive fire
description: The fire becomes irregular (by vāta), sharp (by pitta) or weak (by kapha); balanced doṣas give a balanced fire (AHS Sū 1.8); when the fire is extinguished one dies (Ca Ci 15.4).

name: 'I'-making and 'mine'-making
description: Grasping at 'I' and 'mine', which arises from grasping at the aggregates and brings action and birth; its ceasing ends grasping and birth.

name: The sense of 'I' (ahaṃkāra)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One whose self is deluded by the sense of 'I' thinks 'I am the doer' while actions are done by the guṇas of prakṛti (3.27); the one who, without 'mine' and without 'I', has abandoned all desires attains peace (2.71).
antidotes: knowing the truth of the division of guṇas and actions (3.28)
the conviction 'I am not the doer'

The 'I' that leaves no room in the narrow lane of love; the self that must be erased (āpā meṭe) for Hari to be.

name: Ego-sense and the roots of engagement (Caraka)
description: Engagement rooted in delusion, desire, aversion and karma grows into ego-sense, attachment, doubt, false identification, possessiveness, wrong conviction, non-discrimination and wrong means (Ca Śā 5.10).

name: The false I-notion (ahaṅkāra)
description: The mistaken sense of 'I' regarding body and the like, which ceases through knowledge of the truth about the causes of the faults and through contemplation of the body within.

name: I-making (ahaṅkāra)
description: The constant making of 'I' (SSM 13.19); in Basava's vacana the claim 'I am He' spoken as pride, against which the devotee asks to say 'I am your servant'.

name: The five senses as thieves (aivar)
description: The five senses, pictured by the Āḻvārs as a band that plunders the self, to be put under guard by the Lord's name (Tirumālai 1).

name: Ignorance veiling knowledge (ajñāna)
description: Knowledge is veiled by ignorance, by which beings are deluded (BhG 5.15); the ignorant, faithless doubter perishes (4.40); tamas is born of ignorance (14.8).
antidotes: the Lord's lamp of knowledge, given to those ever yoked who worship him with love (10.10–11)

name: Untimely death
description: Life ending before its measure through exertion beyond strength, wrong eating, excess, bad company, urge suppression, poison and neglect (Ca Vi 3.38; Śā 6.28).

name: The restless mind as demon (akappēy)
description: The mind that runs like a demon or whirls like a fish in a net, to be stilled (Akappēy's refrain; Pattirakiriyār 26); stilling it is the hardest skill (Tāyumāṉavar).

name: Unwholesome thoughts
description: Thoughts of sensuality, ill will and cruelty (MN 19), connected with desire, hatred and delusion (MN 20).

name: Failure to gain a stage (alabdha-bhūmikatva)
description: Vyāsa's gloss: non-attainment of a ground (bhūmi) of samādhi (YBh 1.30).

description: Rasa left uncooked by a weak fire, vitiated and lodged in the stomach, which obstructs the channels (AHS Sū 13.25).

name: Eel-wriggling evasion
description: Refusing to declare anything from fear of false speech, of grasping, of cross-examination, or from dullness.

name: Impatience, intolerance (amarṣa)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: The devotee dear to the Lord is freed from elation, impatience, fear and agitation (12.15).

name: Beginningless latent tendencies (anādi-vāsanā)
description: Liberation is not reached by mere hearing, because beginningless latent tendencies are strong (SS 2.3); hence repeated instruction and practice.

name: Lack of lordship (anaiśvarya)
description: Kauṇḍinya's definition of bondage and his fifth impurity.

name: The four kinds of unwanted things (anartha)
description: Unwanted tendencies arising from past sins, from pious acts (desire for their fruits), from offences, and from devotion itself (desire for gain, honour, prestige); removed in the anartha-nivṛtti stage.
notes: A different fourfold list (svarūpa-bhrama, asat-tṛṣṇā, aparādha, hṛdaya-daurbalya) is given by Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura (recent).

name: Āṇava mala
description: The soul's innate darkness, one substance with many powers, which hides even itself.
alt_description: The twofold impurity of limitation: consciousness losing its freedom, or freedom without consciousness - the loss of one's own nature (ĪPK 3.2.4); 'limited knowledge is bondage' (Śiva Sūtra 1.2).

name: Instability (anavasthitatva)
description: Vyāsa's gloss: the mind's not being established on a ground that has been gained; when samādhi has been attained it would remain established (YBh 1.30).

name: Anger (dveṣa, pratigha)
description: Anger destroys the merit accumulated over thousands of aeons; there is no evil equal to hatred.

name: Clinging to an emptiness of annihilation (chad stong)
description: Taking the ultimate to be a mere nothingness, a non-affirming negation; for the Jonang an extreme that misses the emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects.
antidotes: recognition of the other-empty ultimate through the vajra-yoga

equivalents.note: all Madhyamaka schools reject nihilism, but the Jonang count the rangtong ultimate itself as this error, which the rangtong schools deny

name: Untruth (anṛta)
description: Untruth and breach of ṛta, which Varuṇa punishes with his fetters and from which the vow-taker turns to truth.
notes: rests_on: tea:atharvaveda-saunaka:4.16.2-6, tea:vajasaneyi-samhita:1.5, tea:rgveda:7.86.6

name: Dependence on inference and hearsay (anumān)
description: Accepting scripture, heaven and the gods of the books without verification in the living body.

name: Worship of other gods
description: Bhagavad Gītā 7.20–23, 9.23–25, as the text states it: those whose knowledge is carried off by desires resort to other deities, constrained by their nature; the Lord makes their faith firm and it is he who ordains the fruits they obtain, but the fruit is finite — worshippers of the gods go to the gods. Devotees of other deities who sacrifice with faith sacrifice to him, but not according to the rule; not recognizing him in truth as enjoyer and lord of all sacrifices, they fall.

antidotes: recognizing the Lord in truth as enjoyer of all sacrifices (9.24)
notes: The Gītā does not forbid such worship; it calls it finite in fruit and 'not according to the rule'.
alt_description: Worshipping, remembering or praising gods other than Śiva, or eating their offerings; Basava mocks the crowd of household gods.

name: Belonging to another (anya-śeṣatva)
description: Considering oneself the servant of anyone other than the Lord (including other gods or oneself).

name: Desire for other than Kṛṣṇa (anyābhilāṣa)
description: Any desire other than for Kṛṣṇa's service, and devotion covered by the aims of knowledge (impersonal oneness) or works.

name: Reliance on other supports or other gods (anyāśraya)
description: Single-mindedness is the giving up of other supports (NBS 10); the Āḻvārs reproach those who, though the Lord created all, go worshipping other gods (TVM 4.10.1).
alt_description: Seeking refuge in other gods, paths or worldly supports, which the Puṣṭimārga forbids to those who have taken refuge in Kṛṣṇa.

name: Knowing otherwise (wrong cognition)
description: Misapprehension — the real sense of 'dvaita' in the Māṇḍūkya for Madhva: the soul's wrong knowledge (of its relation to body and Lord), produced by God's will and ceasing by his will when Brahman is known.
antidotes: knowledge of Brahman; the Lord's will

name: Offences in worship (apacāra)
description: Faults of conduct in the Lord's presence and in worship, listed in Vaiṣṇava ritual texts; to be avoided and expiated.

name: Untimely death (apamṛtyu)
description: The danger of death before one's time shown when a period-lord rules the 2nd or 7th house; removed by recitation of the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra and pacification (BPHS 52.2–3).

name: The obstacles to samādhi in the Aparokṣānubhūti
description: Lack of inquiry, laziness, desire for enjoyment, dullness, darkness, distraction, relishing and blankness, to be gradually abandoned by the knower of Brahman.

name: Unwholesome food (apathya) for the practitioner
description: Foods the haṭha texts forbid to the yogin: the bitter, sour, pungent, salty and hot; green vegetables, sour gruel, oil, sesame, mustard; liquor, fish and meat; curds and buttermilk; horse-gram, garlic and asafoetida; food reheated, dry, stale, putrid, over-hot or over-cold; overeating.
antidotes: wholesome food: wheat, rice, barley, milk, ghee, honey, mung, pure water (HYP 1.62-63)

name: Incapacity or indifference (apratipatti)
description: Inability or disinclination to engage in practice even when free of sleep and distraction.

name: Hostility and niggardliness (arāti)
description: The ill-will and meanness of the one who does not give; 'who eats alone has only sin'.
notes: rests_on: tea:rgveda:10.117.1, tea:rgveda:10.117.6, tea:rgveda:8.48.3

name: The six enemies (ariṣaḍvarga)
description: Desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride and envy; the SSM names desire, anger, great delusion, pride and envy as elephants that cannot stand near the lion of Śiva-knowledge.
alt_description: Vārkarī and Rāmānandī usage: lust, anger, greed, delusion, pride and envy — the scorpion's venom of Eknāth's bhāruḍ; the Lord dwells only where they are absent.

name: The six inner enemies (kāma, krodha, lobha, moha, mada, mātsarya)
description: Desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride and envy are to be avoided (PKS 1.19); in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad they, with merit and demerit, are the eight Mothers (Brāhmī and the others) of the first enclosure — to be recognized as powers of the Goddess.

name: Danger to life (ariṣṭa)
description: Configurations threatening early death or calamity, especially of infants (BJ 6; BPHS 9), which may be cancelled by benefic influences (BPHS 10).

name: Arrogance, corruption and laziness (that hinder faith)
description: The arrogant, corrupt and lazy find it hard to believe this teaching; evil beings of wrong views and arrogance find joyful trust the hardest of difficulties.

name: Sorrowful and cruel meditation
description: Brooding on the disagreeable, the agreeable, pain and future reward (ārta), and delighting in violence, falsehood, theft and guarding possessions (raudra); they cause bondage and bad rebirth (TS 9.28–35).

name: Recitation without knowing the meaning
description: Uttering the mantra without its meaning bears no fruit, like oblation on ash; it may even harm (VR 54-56).

name: Falling back after ascending (ārūḍhapatita)
description: Returning to lower ritual practice after taking up Śiva-worship, which makes the worship fruitless.

name: Lust for the formless
description: The seventh fetter: lust for existence in the formless realm.

name: Hope, expectation (āśā)
description: Hope is the great sorrow and freedom from hope the highest happiness, as Piṅgalā learned (MBh 12.168.52).

alt_description: Expectation of gain from others or the world, called the greatest misery; its absence (nairāśya) the greatest happiness.

name: Hope and craving (āśā, tṛṣṇā)
description: Hope in the world and craving, which keep the soul returning; the jīvan-mṛtak is one who has given up hope in the world.

name: Evil meditation (asad-dhyāna)
description: Meditation and mantra used to harm, attract, subjugate or kill others, or meditation on passionate and fearsome forms (Jñānārṇava; YŚ 9).

name: The unbearable offence (asahya-apacāra)
description: Offence that the Lord cannot bear — against him or his devotees without cause, such as envy of the teacher and of the Lord's glory.

name: Incapacity (aśakti): the twenty-eight
description: Injuries of the eleven organs (deafness, blindness, numbness, loss of taste and smell, dumbness, crippled hands, lameness, constipation, impotence, madness) together with seventeen injuries of buddhi — the reversals of the nine contentments and eight accomplishments (SK 49; commentaries).

name: The twenty grounds of disturbed concentration (asamādhi-sthāna)
description: Careless conduct that disturbs concentration — walking hastily, not inspecting the ground, using too large a seat, quarrelling, speaking at wrong times, and so on — listed in the first chapter of the Daśāśrutaskandha.

name: The thirty-three disrespects to the teacher (āśātanā)
description: Faults of a pupil toward teacher and elders — walking ahead of or too close to them, sitting higher, speaking before them, eating first, not answering when called, and so on — listed in the Daśāśrutaskandha.

name: Unwholesome contact of senses and objects
description: Excessive, deficient or wrong contact of the senses with sounds, touches, sights, tastes and smells (Ca Sū 11.37-38; Śā 1.118-128).

name: Renunciation without knowledge or for gain
description: Bearing the wooden staff without knowledge or renouncing for food or fame; such a renouncer 'falls from both worlds' (Paramahaṃsa; Maitreya 2.18–20; Nāradaparivrājaka 5).

description: A list of prides named in the vacanas — commonly of birth, wealth, beauty, youth, learning, power and austerity among them.

name: The eight fetters (aṣṭa-pāśa)
description: Disgust, doubt, fear, shame, loathing, family, conduct and caste; the one bound is a paśu, the one freed is Maheśvara (Kulārṇava 13.90–91).
antidotes: the guru who removes the fetters
alt_description: Disgust, doubt, fear, shame, contempt, family, conventional conduct and caste: bound by them one is a paśu, freed from them one is Maheśvara; the supreme guru removes them (Kulārṇava 13.90-91).

name: The three inauspicious soul-colourings
description: Black, blue and grey leśyās, the colouring of cruel and sorrowful states (TS 3.3; Gommaṭasāra).

name: Impure metallic and mineral preparations

description: Savoring dhyāna and samādhi without skillful means is the bodhisattva's bondage.

name: Attachment to meditative experiences
description: Grasping at bliss, clarity or non-thought leads to rebirth in the desire, form or formless realms rather than to liberation; the experiences are to be released.

name: Attachment to supernatural powers
description: Expecting or using powers as signs of awakening; Jinul calls them 'uncanny matters', the trivial edge of sainthood.

name: Attachment to the radiant citta
description: The subtle attachment to the luminous, seemingly perfect mind at the last stage of practice, in which ignorance still hides.
antidotes: investigating the radiant citta itself with wisdom

name: Attachment to the rewards of ritual (vedavāda)
description: Delight in the Vedic words that promise heaven, enjoyment and power keeps the resolute understanding from being established in samādhi (BhG 2.42–44); those who seek heaven by the three Vedas return when their merit is spent (9.20–21).
antidotes: being free of the three guṇas (2.45)
knowing the teaching, which passes beyond ritual merit (8.28)

name: Attachment to saṃsāra (the three realms)
description: Wishing for the happiness of any rebirth in saṃsāra, which prevents renunciation.
antidotes: contemplating the sufferings of saṃsāra and karma

name: Attachment to stillness (viewing mind, viewing purity, sitting motionless)
description: Fixing the mind to view stillness or purity, suppressing thoughts and sitting motionless as if this were the Way; it binds one with purity and makes one like an insentient thing.
antidotes: the straight mind in all activities

name: Attachment to this life
description: Concern with the eight worldly concerns of this life, which makes even ethics, study and meditation non-dharma.

equivalents.note: the eight concerns are its content

name: Devotion to self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga)
description: The extreme of tormenting the body, practised by the naked ascetics and by the Bodhisatta before his awakening, painful and not conducive to knowledge.
antidotes: the middle way; the pleasure of absorption that is not sensual (MN 36)

name: Overeating (atyāhāra)
description: Eating too much; first of the six destroyers (HYP 1.15); listed among things to avoid (SS 3.33; DYŚ 65).

name: Desire (avā)
description: The seed of unending births (Kuṟaḷ 361); its abandonment gives the unchanging state (370).

name: The passion-producing notion of the whole
description: The notion of a body as an attractive whole ('woman', 'man') with its embellishments, which increases passion and the faults.

name: Ignorance (avidyā)
description: Taking the impermanent, impure, painful and not-self to be permanent, pure, pleasant and self (YS 2.5). Vyāsa's illustrations: taking the earth, sky and heaven-dwellers to be lasting; taking the body to be pure; taking pain for pleasure; taking the not-self (external instruments, the body, the mind) for self; and rejoicing at the prosperity or grieving at the ruin of what is not the self as if it were one's own. It is a positive contrary cognition, not mere absence of knowledge (like 'non-friend' and 'cow-track'); it is the field of the other four afflictions and the seed of the mass of suffering (YBh 2.4, 2.5, 2.15). Its cause is the latent tendency of erroneous knowledge (YBh 2.24).

description: Resting in a thought-free blankness mistaken for realisation; Sakya Paṇḍita says a fool's Mahāmudrā of this kind leads to animal rebirth, the formless realm or the śrāvaka cessation; the Gelug holds that without analysis it cannot become insight.

name: The restless mind
description: The mind agitated by objects wanders in saṃsāra; restlessness is 'being', steadiness the mark of liberation (Jñānakārikā 1.9–10; 2.12–14).

name: Caste pride (cāti)
description: Holding birth-group as real difference; denied by the Siddhars (Sivavākkiyar; Kaṭuveḷi 32).

name: The chain of ruin from dwelling on objects
description: Dwelling on objects breeds attachment; attachment desire; desire anger; anger delusion; delusion loss of memory; loss of memory destruction of the intellect; and so one perishes (BhG 2.62–63).
antidotes: moving among objects free of attraction and aversion (2.64)

name: Clinging to meditative experiences
description: Taking experiences — dream-bliss, the moments and joys, the bliss of the aggregates — for the ultimate, 'brass for gold'; realization without experience, or experience clung to, both fall short.

name: Clinging to meditative experiences and visions
description: Taking experiences, visions or miracles (in dream or waking) as real or as signs of attainment; held as real they are obstacles, known as illusion they become path.

equivalents.note: attachment to powers is one form of it

name: Clinging to words and letters
description: Seeking the meaning in the phrase, reciting texts without understanding, or conversely clinging to 'not using words'.

name: Conceptual thought (vikalpa) as the adverse side
description: Conceptual thought (rnam rtog) is the enemy destroyed by the siddhas' realization — the deer of grasped and grasper shot by Śavaripa, the adverse side torn by Līlapa's ten perfections, the waves stilled by seeing one's mind.

name: Falling away (cyuti)
description: The fourth impurity - the mind's slipping from Rudra; removed with its seed by constant remembrance.

name: Reliance on fate
description: Relying on fate instead of effort, which the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha calls the delusion of the dull.
antidotes: pauruṣa guided by scripture and the good

name: Hypocrisy of the unrealised (dambha)
description: Wearing an ascetic's garb or talking of yoga without practice (HYP 1.65–66; DYŚ 39–46, 'for the sake of penis and belly'); speaking of knowledge before the breath enters the middle path is 'deceitful prattle' (HYP 4.114).

name: Combinations for poverty (daridra-yoga)
description: Configurations of the wealth and gain houses and their lords that bring poverty (BPHS 42).

name: Badness, unwieldiness (dauṣṭhulya)
description: The heaviness and unworkability of body and mind, the substrate of defilement; removed in part by pliancy in meditation and wholly by the transformation of the basis.

name: Dead sitting / 'cold ash and dead wood'
description: Quietist sitting without the life of doubt or insight — 'heretical silent-illumination Chan', 'making a living in the ghost cave' (Dahui; Wumen).

name: Confusion and loss of right mindfulness at death
description: The pains of death ('the wind-knife') scatter the unpractised mind; the presence of those who have taken wine or meat brings loss of right mindfulness and deranged death.

name: Identification with the body
description: The noose by which one is long bound; cut by the sword of knowledge 'I am awareness'.

name: Identification of self with body (dehātma-buddhi)
description: Taking the body as 'I', the grossest form of superimposition, basis of caste, stage and all empirical claims.

name: Taking the body to be the self
description: Virocana concludes from the teaching of the reflected person that the body is the self and teaches the asuras to worship and adorn the body — 'the doctrine of the asuras'; Indra sees that such a self perishes with the body (ChU 8.7-8.9).

name: Slighting a devotee or the guru
description: Overstepping or disrespecting Śiva's devotees or the guru, which destroys life, fortune and the good (Reṇuka's fall for leaping over Dāruka).

name: The urges to be restrained
description: Greed, grief, fear, anger, pride, shamelessness, envy, excessive passion and covetousness, harsh or false speech and acts that harm others — urges which, unlike the natural ones, must be restrained (Ca Sū 7.26-29; AHS Sū 4.24).

name: Merit and demerit as binding (adṛṣṭa)
description: Both merit and demerit bind: engaged in through desire and aversion, they bring about connection with bodies; liberation requires that no new ones arise and the accumulated ones be exhausted.

name: The two nooses of dharma and adharma
description: Dharma leads to heaven and adharma to hell; both bind; cut with the sword of knowledge, one is quickly freed (Jñānakārikā 2.24–28).

name: Seduction to wrong: wine, anger, dice, thoughtlessness (dhruti)
description: Vasiṣṭha's list of what leads one astray against one's own will: surā, manyu, dice, acitti (thoughtlessness); the elder shares the younger's fault; even sleep does not ward off wrong.
antidotes: 'do not play with dice — till your field' (RV 10.34.13)
notes: rests_on: tea:rgveda:7.86.6, tea:rgveda:7.89.5, tea:rgveda:10.34.13

name: Being cheated by those who live off the unseen
description: (As reported) The Lokāyata's obstacle to a happy life: fear of an unseen world and of the fruit of deeds, instilled by priests for whom sacrifice and funeral rites are a livelihood.
antidotes: trusting perception alone; living happily while life lasts

name: Distraction (g.yeng ba)
description: Losing the recognition by following thoughts; non-distraction is 'the main body of meditation'.

name: Distraction
description: A distracted mind does not realize reality; the jewel is lost in the thicket of things; 'without distraction is the king of meditations'.

name: Speculative views
description: Views about self and world — the sixty-two grounds (DN 1), the ten undeclared (MN 72) — a thicket and fetter of views; the sage does not cling to views (Snp 4.3).
antidotes: understanding their origin in contact and craving (DN 1)

name: The net of views (diṭṭhijāla)
description: Speculative views about past and future, in sixty-two grounds, in which every theorist is caught; they are only the feeling of those who do not know, conditioned by contact and craving.
antidotes: understanding the arising, passing, gratification, danger and escape of feeling and contact (DN 1)

name: Spirit harm (gdon)
description: Harm from spirits: in Sowa Rigpa a condition and a class of disease requiring ritual; in Chöd, beings to be fed and repaid rather than fought.

equivalents.note: Āyurvedic seizure by spirits

name: Hate (dosa)
description: Vism XIV: hate (dosa) is that by which one hates, or which hates, or mere hating; its mark is ferocity, like a struck snake; its function is to spread, like a fall of poison, or to burn its own support, like a forest fire; its manifestation is fury, like a foe who has found his chance; its proximate cause is the grounds of resentment; to be regarded as urine mixed with poison. Vism IX opens with reflection on the danger in hate and the benefit of patience before loving-kindness is developed.

name: Doubting the Buddha's wisdom

names.name: giwaku; doubt keeps us in birth-and-death (Shōshinge on Hōnen)

description: Cultivating merit and aspiring to birth while doubting the Buddha's inconceivable wisdom: such beings are born in the womb-palace or borderland, not seeing the Buddha for five hundred years; if one plants good roots but doubts, the lotus does not open.
antidotes: clear faith in the Buddha's wisdom (Larger Sūtra)

equivalents.note: doubt as a hindrance vs doubt of the Buddha's vow specifically

name: Deceit, injury (druh)
description: Deceitful harm and treachery, among the wrongs one asks Varuṇa to remove.
notes: rests_on: tea:rgveda:7.86.5

name: Dualistic grasping (gzung 'dzin)
description: Grasping at apprehended object and apprehending subject, the root of attachment and aversion; when it collapses the illusory body is realized (Karṇatantravajrapada).

name: The three kinds of suffering (Pāśupata account)
description: Suffering of the self (bodily illnesses; mental states such as anger, greed, delusion, fear, despondency, envy, hatred, pride), from beings and from the gods; also womb, birth, ignorance, old age and death. Their final removal is the end of suffering.

name: Bad company (duḥsaṅga)
description: Association with the worldly and faithless, which breeds desire, anger, delusion, loss of memory, loss of understanding and utter ruin; these begin as ripples and become an ocean through association (NBS 43–45).

equivalents.note: the passions it breeds — desire, anger, delusion (cf. BhG 2.62–63; 3.37)

name: Bad dreams (duḥṣvapna)
description: Evil dreams, 'Yama's instrument', warded off by hymns (AVŚ 6.46; RV 2.28.10).
notes: rests_on: tea:atharvaveda-saunaka:6.46.1-2

name: False scriptures
description: Texts contrary to the true scriptures, by which Janārdana is not known; some are said to have been produced to delude.

name: Bad company (duḥsaṅga)
description: Association with the sensual and unrighteous, which destroys truth, purity and calm and returns one to darkness.

name: The attitude of duality
description: One who makes duality is carried off by the yoginīs; abandoning duality one lives by non-dual conduct (KJN 11.3–4).

name: The pairs of opposites (dvandva)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 7.27–28: the delusion of the pairs (dvandva-moha), arising from desire and aversion, into which all beings fall at birth; those of meritorious deeds whose sin has ended are freed from it and worship the Lord.

alt_description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Aversion (dveṣa), set together with passion in each sense towards its object, is a waylayer; one should not come under its sway (3.34). The self-governed person moves among objects with senses free of attraction and aversion and attains serenity (2.64); the one of steady wisdom neither rejoices nor hates (na dveṣṭi) on meeting the pleasant or unpleasant (2.57).
Aversion follows on pain (2.8).
Bhagavad Gītā 5.3: the constant renunciant is the one who neither hates (dveṣṭi) nor desires.
Bhagavad Gītā 7.27: with desire (icchā), the source of the delusion of the pairs that bewilders all beings at birth.
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: The dear devotee hates no being (adveṣṭā sarvabhūtānām) (12.13) and neither rejoices nor hates (12.17); the one who comes to the Lord is without enmity toward any being (11.55).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Aversion is listed among the contents of the field (13.7); the one beyond the guṇas does not hate illumination, activity and delusion when they are present (14.22).
antidotes: Senses free of passion and aversion (2.64)

name: Aversion (dveṣa)
description: Aversion to the disagreeable, arising from false knowledge.

name: Twofold ignorance (the two coverings)
description: Two beginningless coverings in each soul — one hiding the soul's own nature and qualities, the other hiding its knowledge of the Supreme; the Lord destroys the first and removes the second when he grants liberation.

equivalents.note: Same word as Advaita's avidyā, but for Dvaita a real covering removed by grace, not a superimposition on Brahman.

name: The obstacles at the start of practice (Dattātreyayogaśāstra)
description: Laziness, boasting, the company of rogues, mantra-sādhana, alchemy (dhātuvāda) and talk of food — mirages to be recognized and abandoned (DYŚ 47–48).

name: Harm by the eight classes of gods and spirits (lha srin sde brgyad)
description: Illness and misfortune attributed to disturbed local gods and spirits, addressed by smoke and torma offerings, ransom rites and protector practice.

name: The eight intrusive circumstances and eight incompatible propensities
description: Circumstances that suddenly destroy the freedoms (disturbance by the five poisons, stupidity, a false teacher, laziness, a flood of bad karma, servitude, practice only for protection, hypocrisy) and propensities that cut off the chance of liberation (worldly ties, bad character, no disgust with saṃsāra, no faith, delight in wrongdoing, no interest in Dharma, broken vows, broken samaya).
notes: Member lists from memory of the Words of My Perfect Teacher.

name: The eight worldly conditions
description: Gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain, which turn the world (AN 8.6); a mind unshaken by them is a blessing (Snp 2.4).
alt_description: Kagyu contribution: gain and loss, pleasure and pain, praise and blame, fame and disgrace — the 'eight worldly dharmas' Milarepa urges renouncing; self-liberated through the illusory body.

name: The eight prides (mada)
description: Pride in knowledge, honour, family, caste, power, wealth, austerity and body, which spoil right view (Ratnakaraṇḍa); self-praise binds low status (TS 6.25).

name: The eight bonds (aṣṭa-pāśa)
description: The eight fetters beginning with disgust, whose destruction is liberation while living (Dīpikā on YH 1.86); the guru burns the disciple's bonds at initiation (PKS 1.36).
antidotes: knowledge of the cakra-code through the guru
notes: Only 'beginning with disgust' is checked; the full list is the common Kaula one (Kulārṇava), recalled from memory.

name: The eight worldly concerns
description: Gain and loss, pleasure and pain, praise and blame, fame and disrepute: practice stained by them is not dharma (Eight Verses 8; Parting 1).
notes: Contribution of U47.
alt_description: Gain and loss, pleasure and pain, praise and blame, fame and disgrace: the preliminaries turn the mind from them; they disqualify a disciple (Kunjed Gyalpo ch.83).
Gain and loss, pleasure and pain, fame and disgrace, praise and blame, which the wise treat as equal.

name: Haribhadra's eight faults of the mind in yoga
description: Fatigue, anxiety, distraction, agitation, confusion, delight in other things, pain and attachment, removed one by one through the eight views (YDS 16).

equivalents.note: Both are lists of obstacles to yoga; the items differ.

name: The eighteen faults of a monastery
description: Features that make a dwelling unsuitable for developing concentration.

name: The eighteen sources of sin (pāpa-sthānaka)
description: Recited in Śvetāmbara confession: violence, falsehood, theft, unchastity, possessiveness, anger, pride, deceit, greed, attachment, aversion, quarrelling, false accusation, slander, pleasure and displeasure, disparaging others, deceitful falsehood, and the thorn of wrong faith.

name: One-sided dogmatism (ekānta)
description: Holding one aspect or standpoint as the whole truth — the root of rival doctrines and of sectarian quarrel; the Adhyātma critics apply it also to one-sided niścaya and one-sided vyavahāra (Āptamīmāṃsā; Jñānasāra 16; Mokṣamārga Prakāśaka).

name: Sin and offence (enas, āgas)
description: Faults against the gods' ordinances and against fellow men — one's own, bodily, inherited from the fathers, known and unknown — that must be loosened.

name: The three desires (for sons, wealth and worlds)
description: Knowers of the self rise above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth and the desire for worlds and live as mendicants; 'the desire for sons is the desire for wealth, and the desire for wealth is the desire for worlds' (BAU 3.5.1, 4.4.22).

name: The two extremes: eternalism and annihilationism
description: 'It is' is the grasp of permanence and 'it is not' the view of annihilation; whoever accepts real existents falls into one or the other.
antidotes: the middle way of dependent origination

name: Excess or deficiency in eating and sleeping
description: Yoga is not for one who eats too much, nor for one who does not eat at all, nor for one given to too much sleep, nor for one who keeps awake (6.16).

name: Falling to the level of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas
description: For a bodhisattva, realizing the reality-limit before his roots are ripe or lacking wisdom and skillful means — like a wingless bird or an unbaked pot.

name: Abandoning ritual out of false learning
description: The half-learned who needlessly abandon ritual, thinking themselves learned, go to hell (Kulārṇava 9.130) — the counterweight to the realized Kaula's freedom from injunction (9.58).

name: The false or worldly guru
description: Gurus who rob disciples of wealth, know only petty spells, or give 'what is other than the self' are many; the guru who removes suffering is rare (Kulārṇava 13.104-108).
alt_description: A teacher without pure vows, learning, compassion or experience, chosen for fame; following such a teacher is likened to tying a millstone round one's neck.

name: Faulty pronunciation and barbarous speech
description: A mantra wrong in accent or sound fails and harms the sacrificer (PŚ 52; ŚB 1.6.3.10); incorrect words are 'barbarian' and brought the Asuras' defeat (ŚB 3.2.1.23–24; Mahābhāṣya).

name: Fear on hearing the profound teaching
description: Being frightened when hearing that all dharmas are empty and like illusions.

name: The fifteen evils rooted in wealth
description: Theft, violence, falsehood, hypocrisy, lust, anger, arrogance, pride, divisiveness, enmity, distrust, rivalry and the vices (women, gambling, drink), all rooted in wealth.

name: The fifty demonic states of the aggregates
description: States arising as each aggregate is penetrated in meditation — visions, lights, excessive compassion, boldness, elation, false views of nirvāṇa, possession-like states — which lead astray if taken as sagehood.
antidotes: not taking the state as sagehood

names.name: wuni 五逆 — excluded in the 18th vow yet admitted in the lowest grade

description: Killing mother, father or an arhat, dividing the Saṅgha, wounding a Buddha with evil intent; they ripen in hell in the next life; the schism-lie is the gravest.

name: The five causes of bondage
description: Wrong view, non-abstinence, carelessness, passion and activity (TS 8.1).

name: The five evils, five pains and five burnings
description: The Larger Sūtra's account of the evils of this world and their painful and burning retributions, among which the Buddha teaches: (1) the strong oppress the weak, killing and devouring one another; (2) family members and officials without righteousness deceive, cheat and covet; (3) lust and illicit desire; (4) double tongue, harsh words, lies, frivolous talk, slander of the good, unfilial conduct; (5) idleness, neglect of family and parents, and indulgence in drink and food.
notes: Openings of the five sections read locally in T360; content summarised from their opening lines.

name: The five faults of calm abiding
description: Laziness, forgetting the instruction, sinking and agitation, non-application (of the remedy) and over-application (applying it when not needed) — the obstacles to stability of mind.
alt_description: Laziness, forgetting the instruction, laxity and excitement, non-application and over-application.
notes: Contribution of U47.

name: The five faults of yoga (Mokṣadharma)
description: Desire, anger, greed, fear and sleep — the five faults of yoga that the seers know, to be cut off (MBh 12.232.4; also 12.266.14).

name: The five faults removed by the buddha-nature teaching
description: Discouragement, contempt for inferior beings, grasping the unreal, denying the real dharma, excessive self-love.

name: The five higher fetters
description: Lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness and ignorance, abandoned at arahantship.

name: The five hindrances (nīvaraṇa)
description: In Vism IV (commentary on 'quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unwholesome states'), the 'unwholesome states' from which the first jhāna is secluded are the hindrances, because they are the adversaries and opposites of the jhāna factors: concentration is the opposite of sensual desire, rapture of ill will, applied thought of sloth and torpor, happiness of restlessness and remorse, sustained thought of doubt (cited from the Peṭaka). The jhāna does not arise while they are unabandoned, so they are called the factors of abandoning (five factors abandoned). They are abandoned by suppression (vikkhambhana), and 'seclusion' (viveka) is the going away of the hindrances. Ch. XXII lists them among the states to be abandoned, so called by way of covering, hindering and concealing consciousness.

Sensual desire, malice, torpor-and-sleepiness, restlessness-and-remorse, doubt; in the Kośa, belonging to the desire realm, destroying the aggregates of morality, concentration and wisdom.

The Pali Abhidhamma adds ignorance as a sixth hindrance.

name: The five sheaths of limitation (kañcuka)
description: Limited agency (kalā), limited knowledge (vidyā), attachment (rāga), time (kāla) and restriction (niyati), which with māyā make the inner covering of the individual: 'only now, only a little, only this, I know with all of myself' (Paramārthasāra 16-17).

name: The five afflictions (kleśa)
description: Ignorance (avidyā), I-am-ness (asmitā), attachment (rāga), aversion (dveṣa) and clinging to life (abhiniveśa) (YS 2.3); Vyāsa: 'the five errors' (viparyaya), which he names darkness, delusion, great delusion, gloom and blind gloom (YBh 1.8). Active, they make firm the office of the guṇas, keep transformation going, raise the stream of cause and effect and, interdependent, bring karma to ripening (YBh 2.3). Ignorance is their field; each is dormant, attenuated, interrupted or fully active, and the burnt-seed state belongs to the last body only (YS 2.4, YBh 2.4). The store of karma is rooted in them (YS 2.12) and ripens while they exist (YS 2.13).

name: The five lower fetters
description: Identity view, doubt, clinging to rules and vows, sensual lust and ill will, latent even in an infant; abandoned by the non-returner through jhāna and insight (MN 64).

name: The five malas
description: Āṇava, karma, māyā, māyeya and tirodhāna (Tamil list); Sanskrit lists vary (bindu for the pure worlds).

name: The five sins
description: Violence, falsehood, stealing, unchastity and possessiveness, from which the vows abstain (TS 7.1, 7.13–17).

name: The five poisons (dug lnga)
description: Desire, anger, ignorance (dullness), pride and jealousy, which lead to the realms and are, when recognized, the five wisdoms.

name: The five thieves
description: Lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride, which rob the house of the body; the guru frees the disciple from them (Sahajobāī).

equivalents.note: Five of the six enemies (envy omitted).

name: The five turbidities (pañcakaṣāya)
description: Degeneracy of the aeon, beings, defilements, views and lifespan, in which the Buddha teaches by skillful means.

names.name: wuzhuo e'shi 五濁惡世 — the age in which only the Pure Land gate is passable

name: The five (wrong) views
description: Satkāya-view (self and mine), view of extremes (permanence/annihilation), wrong view (denial of cause and result), attachment to views, attachment to rules and observances; belief in Īśvara as cause belongs to the last.

name: The five obstacles (virodhi-pañcaka)
description: Obstacles to knowing one's own nature, to knowing the Lord's supremacy, to the means, to the goal, and to attainment.

name: The fivefold ignorance
description: Tamas, moha, mahāmoha, tāmisra and andhatāmisra - ignorance in five divisions, the first thing to arise from the creator (VP 1.5.5).

name: The four afflictions of the afflicted mind
description: Self-view, self-delusion, self-conceit and self-love, which always accompany the seventh consciousness.

name: The four biases (agati)
description: Doing evil through desire, hatred, delusion or fear (DN 31).

name: The effluents (āsava)
description: The effluents of sensuality, becoming and ignorance — the usual sutta list of three — with views as a fourth in some lists, abandoned by seven methods (MN 2); their destruction is the knowledge of the arahant (DN 2).
antidotes: the four jhānas and the knowledge of the four truths
the four paths (destruction of the taints)

name: The four dangers to the lineage
description: Habituation to the afflictions, bad friends, deprivation, and dependence on others — which keep one with the bodhisattva lineage from awakening.

name: The four deviations from emptiness (shor sa bzhi)
description: Deviating from the essence of emptiness (not recognizing it), into 'sealing' (labelling things empty), into the antidote (using emptiness as a remedy), and into the path (treating emptiness as something to reach later).

name: The four bodily ties (gantha)
description: Covetousness, ill will, clinging to rules and observances, and dogmatic insistence that 'this alone is true'.

name: The four hundred and four diseases
description: Diseases counted as 4 × 101: karmic (yield only to Dharma), life-span (require treatment), spirit-caused (require ritual) and superficial (pass by themselves or with diet and behaviour).

name: The four passions (krodha, māna, māyā, lobha) with their four varieties
description: Anger, pride, deceit and greed (8.9): counted among the rising states of the soul (2.6), a division of the sāmparāyika inflow (6.5), the ground of conduct-deluding karma (6.14, 8.9), a cause of bondage (8.1) and the reason the soul takes in karma-particles (8.2); each has four varieties, anantānubandhī, apratyākhyāna, pratyākhyāna and saṃjvalana (8.9), which the sūtra names but does not define.

alt_description: Anger, pride, deceit and greed — the glue that makes karma stick to the soul — each in four grades from endless-binding to smouldering; their conquest is liberation (YŚ 4.5).
antidotes: forbearance, humility, straightforwardness, contentment (the first four of the ten virtues)

equivalents.note: Overlapping lists of passions; the Jain four include pride and deceit.

name: The four Māras
description: Māra as the aggregates, the defilements, death, and the divine son Māra.
notes: Standard Mahāyāna list (e.g. in the Lalitavistara and Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra); exact sūtra locus not asserted.
alt_description: The demons of the aggregates, afflictions, death and the 'son of the gods' (distraction by pleasure), as obstacles to practice; cut by the kusāli offering and Chöd.
Kagyu contribution: the demons Milarepa met at Red Rock Jewel Valley vanished when recognized as his own mind's projections.

name: The four māras of Chöd
description: The obstructive māra (sense objects that provoke attachment and aversion), the unobstructive māra (arising thoughts), the māra of elation (attachment to attainments and good fortune) and the māra of conceit (self-fixation), the root of the others.
antidotes: cutting self-fixation by the view of emptiness

equivalents.note: same name, different set: the classical four are the aggregates, afflictions, death and the divine son

name: The four notions (self, being, soul, person)
description: Notions whose presence means one is not a bodhisattva.

name: The four obstacles to absorption (laya, vikṣepa, kaṣāya, rasāsvāda)
description: The four faults named by commentators for the Kārikā 3.42–3.45: laya, vikṣepa, kaṣāya, rasāsvāda; the Kārikā gives its own counsel for each.
antidotes: do not relish bliss; be unattached by discernment

alt_description: Dullness (laya), distraction (vikṣepa), latent attachment (kaṣāya) and relishing (rasāsvāda).

name: The four floods
description: Sensuality, becoming, views and ignorance, crossed by the raft of the eightfold path (SN 35.238; SN 1.1).
alt_description: Floods and bonds of sensual desire, existence, views and ignorance, named as clusters in the Abhidhamma matrix.

name: The four defeats (pārājika)
description: Sexual intercourse, taking what is not given, killing a human being, falsely claiming superhuman attainments — the offences that end monkhood; the Kashmiris held the fallen monk to possess both discipline and its loss.

name: The four instincts (saṃjñā)
description: The craving for food, fear, sexual desire and possessiveness found in all worldly beings.

name: The four kinds of clinging (upādāna)
description: Vism XVII, in the treatment of 'feeling as condition of craving': clinging to sensual pleasures, to views, to rites and observances, and to a doctrine of self; 'clinging' is firm grasping (the prefix upa- meaning firm). In brief, clinging to sensual pleasures is the firmness of craving, and the other three are just views; in detail, the firmness of craving of a hundred and eight kinds is the first, tenfold wrong view the second, the grasping that purity comes from rites and observances the third, and the twenty-fold view of a personal existence the fourth. The orders: in arising, the doctrine of self first; in abandoning, views and the rest first (cut by the stream-entry path), sensual clinging last (arahat path); in teaching, sensual clinging first.

alt_description: Clinging to sense pleasures, to views, to rules and observances, to a doctrine of self.
To sensual pleasures, views, rules and vows, and a doctrine of self (SN 12.2; MN 11).

name: The four kinds of idle talk (vikathā)
description: Talk about women, food, country and kings — forms of carelessness to be avoided by ascetics.

name: The four perversions (vipallāsa)
description: Perceiving, thinking and viewing the impermanent as permanent, suffering as happiness, not-self as self and the unattractive as attractive (AN 4.49).

equivalents.note: YS 2.5 defines avidyā with the same four inversions; see brw:buddhism-yoga-four-inversions

alt_description: Taking the impermanent as permanent, the painful as pleasant, the not-self as self and the foul as beautiful — in perception, thought and view.

name: The four inversions (and the Mahāyāna double set)
description: Taking the impermanent, suffering, selfless and impure as permanent, blissful, self and pure; in the Mahāparinirvāṇa and Śrīmālā also taking the Tathāgata's permanence, bliss, self and purity as their opposites.
notes: The first set of four is shared with the Pali vipallāsa (AN 4.49); the reversed set is the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa's and Śrīmālā's addition.

name: The four perversions (viparyāsa)
description: Taking the impermanent as permanent, the painful as pleasant, the impure as pure, and the non-self as self.
antidotes: contemplation of impermanence, suffering, impurity and selflessness (CŚ 1–4)

equivalents.note: Same four perversions.

alt_description: Taking the impermanent as permanent, the painful as pleasant, the impure as pure and the selfless as self; the afflictions arise in dependence on them.

name: The four ways of straying from emptiness (shor sa bzhi)
description: Straying into emptiness as the basic nature of knowables, straying on the path (seeking the fruit elsewhere), straying into emptiness as an antidote, and straying into sealing appearances with emptiness.
notes: Member list from memory (with the 'three deviations', gol sa gsum, into the three realms).

name: The fourteen unwholesome mental factors
description: The unwholesome factors of the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha: delusion, shamelessness, fearlessness of wrongdoing, restlessness; greed, wrong view, conceit; hatred, envy, avarice, remorse; sloth, torpor; doubt.

name: Birth at a junction (gaṇḍānta)
description: Birth at the junction of Jyeṣṭhā and Mūla, Āśleṣā and Maghā, or Revatī and Aśvinī, which endangers the father or the child; requires pacification (BPHS 94).

name: The twenty-five faults of singers
description: Faults that make a singer censured — biting the teeth, shouting, hissing, fear, hesitation, trembling, gaping, a crow-like voice, losing the tāla, off-pitch notes, inattention, nasality and the rest (ŚR 3.24–26); in the body, certain petals on which the jīva rests destroy success in music (ŚR 1.2.140–144).

name: The destructive karmas
description: Knowledge-obscuring, perception-obscuring, deluding and obstructive karma, which veil the soul's own qualities; their destruction yields omniscience (TS 10.1).

name: Languor (glāni)
description: Weariness, a 'robber in the body', arising from ignorance and removed by the opening-out (unmeṣa) of spanda (SK 3.8).

name: Planetary affliction (graha-pīḍā)
description: The trouble a badly placed planet brings in its period or transit — the ripening of past karma which the planets, as forms of Janārdana, deliver; happiness and sorrow of all creatures depend on them.

name: Seizure by spirits (graha)
description: Seizure by the eight classes of beings shows as superhuman knowledge and action; for Caraka it strikes only one already self-struck by prajñāparādha (Su Utt 60; Ca Ni 7.10-22). Summary only.
antidotes: good conduct and holding oneself the agent of one's pleasure and pain (Ca Ni 7.22)

name: Birth during an eclipse
description: Those born during a solar or lunar eclipse face disease, hardship, poverty and fear of death (BPHS 91.1).

name: Grasping at nirvāṇa
description: The thought 'without grasping I shall attain nirvāṇa; nirvāṇa will be mine' is itself a great grasping.

name: Grasping at extremes
description: Grasping at existence, non-existence, both or neither — even at emptiness — which is the absence of the view.
antidotes: resting in the view free of extremes

equivalents.note: grasping emptiness as a view is one form of it

name: The gross downfalls
description: Secondary breaches of the tantric vow, listed after the root downfalls in the Advayavajrasaṃgraha.

name: The ground (entrenchment) of ignorance (avidyāvāsabhūmi)
description: The beginningless subtle ignorance remaining in arhats and pratyekabuddhas, removed only by buddhas.

name: Bondage by the three guṇas
description: The guṇas bind the embodied one: sattva by attachment to happiness and knowledge, rajas by attachment to action, tamas by negligence, sloth and sleep (BhG 14.5–8); attachment to the guṇas causes birth in good and evil wombs (13.21).
antidotes: seeing no agent but the guṇas (14.19)
taking refuge in the Lord alone (7.14)
seeing no agent but the guṇas and knowing what is higher than them (14.19)
serving the Lord with the unswerving yoga of devotion (14.26)
members: sattva: attachment to happiness and knowledge
sattva: attachment to happiness (sukha-saṅga) and to knowledge (jñāna-saṅga)

Bhagavad Gītā 14.5–9: sattva, rajas and tamas, born of prakṛti, bind the imperishable embodied one in the body — sattva by attachment to happiness and to knowledge, rajas by attachment to action, tamas by heedlessness, idleness and sleep; attachment to the guṇas causes births in good and bad wombs (13.22).

name: Seeing merit and fault
description: Seeing things in terms of merit and fault is itself the fault; being beyond both is the merit.

name: Slandering and turning from the guru
description: The tāmasa disciple slanders the guru, looks for faults and turns away, and is 'dead while living' (Kubjikāmata 12.5-9); when the guru is angry no one can protect (Kulārṇava 12.49).

name: Blaming the guru
description: Blame of the guru is condemned; through such a lapse the scripture fell into the ocean (KJN 16.54).

name: Combustion of Jupiter or Venus
description: While Jupiter or Venus is set in the sun's rays, marriages, sacred-thread ceremonies and similar rites are not performed (muhūrta texts).

name: Hatred of Hari and his devotees
description: Hostility to Viṣṇu and to those devoted to him, through which souls fit for darkness quickly reach blinding darkness; rejecting the Supreme though the wise are present seals it.

name: Elation (harṣa)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: The devotee dear to the Lord is freed from elation, impatience, fear and agitation (12.15) and does not rejoice (na hṛṣyati) (12.17).

name: Secret teachings (hiji bōmon)
description: Teachings transmitted in secret at night outside the public teaching (as Zenran claimed); rejected by Shinran and Rennyo.

name: Gold, woman and land (honnu, heṇṇu, maṇṇu)
description: The three proverbial objects of attachment for which 'millions died'; Allama teaches that the real bond is the desire before the mind (Akka Mahādēvi, as a woman, speaks rather of worldly husbands).

name: Hope and fear
description: The poison of hope and fear intoxicates the yogin's mind and binds the innate gnosis; the fruit manifests only without them.
alt_description: Hoping for results and fearing failure in practice; 'without hope and fear the fruit is manifest'.
Hoping for results and fearing failure in meditation, which keep the mind in dualistic grasping; the Kunjed Gyalpo counts seeking and accomplishing among the deviations.

name: Hoping for attainments
description: The mind that hopes and asks for accomplishments, removed by knowing that they arise within oneself through dependent arising.

name: A hostile or unsuitable mantra (ari-mantra)
description: A mantra incompatible with the practitioner, detected by the preliminary checks; Kṛṣṇānanda insists on the checks even for the Mahāvidyās because such a fault has been seen (Tantrasāra).

name: The knots of the heart
description: Knots in the heart that bind one to mortality; when they are cut, all doubts vanish and one's actions are exhausted, and the mortal becomes immortal (KU 2.3.15; MuU 2.2.8, 3.2.9); loosened by firm memory arising from pure food and mind (ChU 7.26.2).
antidotes: seeing the higher and the lower (MuU 2.2.8)

name: Imbalance of the three humours
description: Excess or deficiency of vaḷi, aḻal and aiyam causes disease (Kuṟaḷ 941); the tradition counts 4,448 diseases arising from it. Remedied by regimen, medicine and kaṟpam.

name: Recitation without understanding
description: Learning the Veda without its meaning: 'a post that bears loads', 'dry fuel without fire' (Nirukta 1.18); the Veda does not purify one without conduct (VDh 6.3).

name: Imbalance of the faculties
description: Excess faith with weak wisdom, or excess wisdom with weak faith; excess energy (agitation) or excess concentration (idleness); mindfulness is needed everywhere.
antidotes: balancing faith with wisdom and energy with concentration

name: Improper breath-control
description: Wrongly practised breath-control produces hiccup, asthma, cough and pains of head, ears and eyes, and can kill (Yogacūḍāmaṇi 116–118; Śāṇḍilya 1.23).
antidotes: gradual, skilful practice under a guru (HYP 2.15, 2.18)

name: Indulgence in the Kula substances outside the rite
description: Using the Kaula substances for pleasure, without initiation, consecration or instruction — the texts' chief warning: wine gives no perfection by itself; the addicted and wilful go to hell (Kulārṇava 2.117; 5.96-105).

name: Insatiable desire
description: Desire is never quenched by enjoyment but grows like fire fed with ghee (MDh 2.94); the senses must be reined in like horses (MDh 2.88).

name: Intellectual understanding (zhijie)
description: Conceptual understanding taken for awakening; Huineng's rebuke of Shenhui as 'a follower of intellectual understanding'.
alt_description: Intellectual understanding (go ba) and passing experience (myong ba) mistaken for stable realization (rtogs pa).

name: Intoxicants (ganja, opium, toddy)
description: Kaṭuveḷi: do not smoke ganja or drink toddy (29); Pattirakiriyār longs not to wither with ganja, opium and toddy but to drink the fivefold nectar (35).

name: The two deeds (iruviṉai)
description: Good and bad deeds both bind: the Lord drives us 'by the rope of the two deeds' (Tiruttillai 11); one's own deed burns oneself; the knower seeks neither (Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam 13).
alt_description: Good and bad karma alike bind — 'golden and iron chains'; they cease to cling to those who praise the Lord or act as his servants.

name: Envy (issā)
description: Vism XIV, an indeterminate factor in the hate-rooted consciousness: envy is envying; its mark is jealousy of others' success; its function is dissatisfaction with it; its manifestation is turning away from it; its proximate cause is others' success; to be regarded as a fetter.

name: The company of people (janasaṅga)
description: Mixing with people; its abandonment is among the six promoters (HYP 1.15–16).

name: Love that seeks its own pleasure (the paramour's love)
description: Love without knowledge of the Lord's greatness, and without happiness in his happiness, is like the love of paramours; the gopīs' love had neither fault (NBS 22–24).

name: Pride of birth; judging devotees by caste (jāti-abhimāna)
description: Measuring devotees by caste, learning or family: the Āḻvārs teach that the servants of the Lord's servants, even caṇḍālas, are one's masters, and that Veda-learned brāhmaṇas who revile devotees become outcastes; the Nārada Sūtra that no such distinction exists among devotees because they are the Lord's own; the Bhāgavata that a devoted dog-cooker is better than a brāhmaṇa averse to the Lord.
antidotes: remembering that outward birth does not touch devotion (Cokhāmeḷā's sugarcane)

alt_description: Pride in birth, which the saints say kills devotion (Tukārām: 'well that you made me a Kuṇbī, or I would have died of pride') and which excludes the low-born from God's house.

name: The heresy of 'settled ten kalpas ago' (jikkō anjin)
description: The view that birth was already settled when Amida attained buddhahood ten kalpas ago, so that no entrusting is now needed; rejected by Rennyo.

name: Contraction of knowledge (jñāna-saṅkoca)
description: Through karma the soul's attributive consciousness, infinite by nature, is contracted; in release it expands fully.

name: Forgetfulness in sense-life (Matsyendra in the Kadalī kingdom)
description: The guru himself can forget his realisation amid pleasures, as Matsyendra did among the women of the Kadalī kingdom, until awakened by the disciple (Gorakṣavijaya).

name: Desire for lower ends (wealth, power, kaivalya)
description: Seeking from the Lord anything other than himself — wealth, lordly powers or the isolated enjoyment of one's own self — obstructs the highest goal.

name: The snare of Kāl
description: Kāl (Nirañjan, the negative power) keeps souls bound in the three worlds by karma, māyā and false religion, and sends false teachers; freed only by the true Name/Sant Satguru.

name: Fear of Time (death)
description: Kāla (Time/death) devours the unpractised; out of fear of it Brahmā, yogīs and sages practise breath-control; the yogī in samādhi is not devoured by time (GŚ 38, 98).

name: Kāla-sarpa yoga
description: The configuration with all seven planets between Rāhu and Ketu, widely feared in present practice and remedied at pilgrimage sites.
notes: Not found in the classical texts consulted; recorded as recent practice.

name: The five dwellings of Kali
description: Gambling, drinking, illicit women, slaughter and gold, where falsehood, intoxication, lust, passion and enmity reside.

name: The weakness of the Kali age
description: In the Kali age people are afflicted by hunger and sleep and cannot perform full puraścaraṇa (Kālīvilāsa 4.6); Vedic mantras have lost their power (Mahānirvāṇa 2.14-15).

name: False garb (kaḷḷa vēṭam)
description: The hypocrite's ascetic costume: 'do not put on a false garb' (Kaṭuveḷi 33); 'for those who conquered death, why costumes?' (Kuṭampai 26); Pattirakiriyār longs to leave the vain garb for Śiva's (28).

name: Stain, impurity, fault (kalmaṣa, kilbiṣa, pāpa)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: impurities are destroyed by sacrifice (4.30); the worst sinner crosses all wrong by the raft of knowledge (4.36); stains are shaken off by knowledge (5.17) and destroyed in the seers who attain brahma-nirvāṇa (5.25); the one acting with actions placed in Brahman is not stained by sin (5.10); one doing merely bodily action incurs no fault (4.21); the calm yogin is stainless (6.27–28); the striving yogin is cleansed of faults over many births (6.45).

name: Conceptual construction (kalpanā, vikalpa)
description: All conceptions — even meditations on sun, moon and fire and on the gods — keep beings turning like a water-wheel; the schools full of vikalpa do not free from saṃsāra (Jñānakārikā 2.20–23; Akulavīra A.7–10).

name: Turbidity of mind (kaluṣa)
description: Mental turbidity; yoga arises only for one whose mind is unclouded; its removal is the first stage's purification.

name: Desire (kāma)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Desire arises from attachment to objects dwelt on and gives rise to anger (2.62); the ritual-minded are desire-souled (2.43); the one of steady wisdom gives up all desires (2.55, 2.71) and is not 'a desirer of desires' (2.70). alt_description: A person is made of desire; desire leads to resolve, action and its result, and the desiring one returns to this world for action (BAU 4.4.5-6); one who desires desires is born here and there by them (MuU 3.2.2); children pursue outward desires into the net of death (KU 2.1.2); when all desires in the heart are released one becomes immortal (BAU 4.4.7; KU 2.3.14).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: undertakings free of desire mark the learned (4.19); the unyoked is bound, attached to the fruit through the drive of desire (5.12); the surge of desire and anger is to be withstood before leaving the body (5.23); the liberated sage is free of desire (icchā), fear and anger (5.28); the yoked one is free of craving for all desires (6.18); desires born of intention are to be abandoned without remainder (6.24).

Bhagavad Gītā 7.20, 7.22; 9.21: desires carry off people's knowledge so that they resort to other deities for their desires; the followers of the three Vedas, 'desiring desires', obtain only going and coming. (At 7.11 the Lord is desire not opposed to dharma.)
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Those whose desires have turned away (vinivṛtta-kāma) reach the imperishable place (15.5).

Desire for one's own pleasure, the downward current; for the Sahajiyā not to be suppressed but refined into prema, for the Bāuls to be mastered before practice — and the danger into which the unqualified fall.

name: Lust, the disease of the heart
description: Kāma called the heart's disease, cast off by one who hears the rāsa-līlā with faith.

name: Desire and anger, the enemy (kāma–krodha)
description: Desire, and anger with it, born of rajas, all-devouring, is the constant enemy of the wise; it covers knowledge as smoke covers fire and has the senses, mind and intellect as its seat (BhG 3.36–43).

name: Desire and poison (kāma-viṣa)
description: From the seed comes desire, which is creation, and from desire poison, which is death (AmŚ 43–44); desire is longing for objects (Candrāvalokana).

name: Sensual desire (kāmacchanda)
description: First hindrance. In Vism IV it is the desire that the jhāna opposes: concentration is its opposite (p. 141), and 'quite secluded from sensual desires' declares the seclusion of suppression of sensual desire. The text distinguishes objective sensual desires (vatthukāma: agreeable sights, sounds etc.) and sensual desires as defilement (kilesakāma: zeal, lust, zealous lust, intention, lust for sense objects). How it obstructs, in the text's words: consciousness enticed by objects of many kinds is not concentrated on a unified object, and, overcome by sensual desire, does not follow the way to abandon the sense sphere.

name: Excess of fat and phlegm
description: An excess of fat (medas) or phlegm (śleṣman) calls for the six acts before breath-control; those whose humours are balanced need not do them (HYP 2.21, 2.36).

name: Aggravation of kapha
description: Kapha increases by day-sleep, lack of exercise, idleness, sweet, sour, salt, cold, unctuous, heavy and slimy foods, especially in the cold seasons and spring, in the morning and evening and just after meals; increased, it brings whiteness, coldness, heaviness, lethargy and excess sleep.

name: Defect in the causes of cognition
description: A defect in the conditions producing a cognition (e.g. in the sense organ), knowledge of which, or a contradicting cognition, sets aside a cognition's intrinsic validity.

name: Beginningless karma as bondage (avidyā-karma)
description: Merit and demerit from beginningless time bind the soul to bodies in prakṛti and contract its knowledge; this karma is what scripture calls avidyā.

name: Karma as bond
description: The beginningless stream of good and bad deeds binding the soul to birth.

name: The fault of kārpaṇya (pitiable weakness)

antidotes: The text's counsel: know it (vijānīyāt); when evenness is reached do not stir it (3.44).

name: The faults of poetry (kāvya-doṣa)
description: Faults of word, sentence, meaning and rasa that diminish poetry — rasa's soul is harmed by naming a rasa directly, by impropriety and the like (SD 1.3; KP 7).

name: Mortification of the body (kāyakleśa)
description: Ascetic practices that torment the body — early-morning (cold) bathing, fasting, eating once a day or not at all — which the haṭha texts tell the beginner to avoid (Gorakṣa's saying in HYP 1.61; GS 5.31; ŚS 3.33 lists early bathing and fasting among what obstructs yoga). name: Kemadruma yoga
description: The lunar combination with no planet on either side of the Moon, which brings poverty and misery unless cancelled (BJ 13).

name: Reliance on bare reasoning
description: Trying to know Viṣṇu by reasoning alone or by the senses, apart from the true scriptures; 'devotion to bad reasoning' (kutarka) is named among the asuras' traits.

name: Gross and subtle activities of the afflictions
description: The gross activities of the afflictions are thinned by kriyā-yoga and abandoned by meditation as discerning insight; the subtle ones (seeds) are abandoned by involution (pratiprasava). As gross dirt is shaken from cloth first and fine dirt removed later with effort, the gross activities have small opposition and the subtle ones great (YS 2.10–2.11, YBh 2.11).

name: Greed (lobha)
description: Vism XIV, in the consciousness rooted in greed: greed (lobha) is that by which one is greedy, or which is greedy, or mere greed; its mark is grasping an object, like a monkey-lime; its function is sticking, like a piece of meat in a hot pan; its manifestation is non-relinquishing, like lamp-black dye; its proximate cause is seeing enjoyment in things that fetter. Craving growing as a river is to be regarded as a fast stream to the ocean, taking one to the states of loss. Vism III gives the greedy temperament (rāgacarita) its own marks (phn:vism-carita-raga).

Vism XXII counts it fivefold: over dwelling, family, gain, teaching and praise.

description: The Evil One, who tempts and threatens practitioners and finds his opening in those who roam outside their own pasture (SN 47.6; SN 4; SN 5).

name: Māra's deeds against the perfection of wisdom
description: Slowness or scattering of eloquence, yawning and laughing while copying, weariness, turning to lesser sūtras, false visions of the Buddha denying the teaching.

name: Envy (matsara)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 4.22: the one free of envy (vimatsara), content with what comes unsought and beyond the opposites, is not bound though acting.

name: 'I and mine' as māyā
description: The sense of 'I' and 'mine', 'you' and 'yours' is the māyā that holds all beings (Rāma to Lakṣmaṇa).

name: Māyā the swindler
description: Māyā, the great swindler with the noose of the three qualities, who appears in every house in a different form — wealth, the goddess, the idol, the pilgrim-water — and binds all creatures.

name: Māyā
description: Śiva's concealing power by which difference is imagined; personified in the Prabhuliṅgalīle as Māyā sent to seduce Allama; Allama locates it in the mind's desire, not in gold, woman or land.

name: Māyīya mala (the impurity of difference)
description: The appearance of the knowable as separate, which gives birth and experience (ĪPK 3.2.5).
alt_description: The bond of māyā's products — body, organs, worlds — which also help the soul by partly awakening it.

name: Mere non-thought mistaken for wisdom
description: Cultivating the mere absence of recollection and attention without correct analysis; like fainting, it only cultivates delusion and cannot remove the obscurations.

name: Wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi)
description: Vism XIV: wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) is that by which one sees wrongly; its mark is unwise insistence; its function is clinging; its manifestation is wrong adherence; its proximate cause is the wish not to see the noble ones and the like; to be regarded as the most blameworthy. Vism XXII lists it among the wrongnesses (micchatta) and as the sense of 'adherence' (parāmāsa).

name: Mistaking the all-base for awareness
description: Resting in a blank, indifferent, thoughtless state — the all-base (kun gzhi) — and taking it for the dharmakāya; Longchenpa warns that this leads to the formless realms, not to liberation.

name: Hypocritical restraint (mithyācāra)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One who restrains the organs of action but sits dwelling in mind on sense-objects is called a hypocrite (3.6); contrasted with one who controls the senses by the mind and undertakes karma-yoga unattached (3.7).
antidotes: Control the senses by the mind and act unattached (3.7)

name: False knowledge (mithyājñāna)
description: The first impurity; removed by the living with the teacher and learning (vāsa).

name: False knowledge (mithyājñāna)
description: The root of the series leading to birth and pain: taking the non-self as self, denying the self, taking pain as pleasure, the impermanent as permanent, the unprotecting as protection, the fearful as safe, the loathsome as desirable; denying karma, its fruit and rebirth; fearing liberation.

equivalents.note: Yoga's avidyā (YS 2.5) has an overlapping list of misapprehensions.

name: Wrong view (mithyātva)
description: Belief contrary to the realities, the first and root cause of bondage; five kinds (one-sided, contrary, indiscriminate reverence, doubt, ignorance — Digambara list) or innate and acquired.
antidotes: right view through the three processes and the breaking of the knot
alt_description: Wrong faith, of five kinds: one-sided, perverse, doubting, vainayika and ajñānika; or, as taught by others, the four vāda classes (363 views).
notes: U33 contribution; U35 owns the Jain account.

name: Mixed (miscellaneous) practice
description: Abandoning exclusive practice for mixed practices: mind disturbed by conditions, not in accord with the vow, recollection not continuous, dedication not earnest, passions intervening, no shame or repentance, no gratitude, pride and pursuit of fame, no good companions — hardly one or two in a hundred are born; the mixed stop in the land of sloth.

name: Delusion (moha)
description: Vism XIV: delusion (moha) is that by which one is deluded, or which is deluded, or mere delusion; its mark is blindness of consciousness or lack of knowledge; its function is non-penetration or concealing the nature of the object; its manifestation is wrong practice or darkness; its proximate cause is unwise attention; it is the root of all that is unwholesome.

alt_description: Delusion, born of anger (BhG 2.63) and of the pairs of opposites (7.27), by which the world does not know the Lord (7.13); destroyed by knowledge and grace (4.35; 18.73).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna's mind is bewildered about dharma (2.7); understanding must cross the thicket of delusion (2.52); delusion arises from anger and confuses memory (2.63); those deluded by the guṇas are attached to their actions (3.29); those who cavil are deluded in all knowledge (3.32); desire deludes the embodied one through the senses, mind and understanding (3.40). The one in the brahmic state is not bewildered (2.72).

Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: the whole world, deluded by the three guṇa-made states, does not recognize the Lord (7.13); the deluded (mūḍha) evil-doers do not take refuge in him (7.15); the deluded world does not know him, veiled by yoga-māyā (7.25); all beings fall into bewilderment at birth through the delusion of the pairs (7.27); the deluded disregard him in human form (9.11) and resort to a deluding nature (9.12).
The third unwholesome root, one of the three fires.

Knowledge taught by the truth-seers frees one from falling into delusion again (4.35); creatures are deluded because knowledge is covered by ignorance (5.15); the knower of Brahman is undeluded (5.20).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Arjuna declares his delusion gone through the supreme secret teaching called adhyātma (11.1); the Lord bids him not be bewildered (vimūḍhabhāva) at the terrible form (11.49); one who knows the Lord as unborn and beginningless is undeluded among mortals (10.3); freedom from delusion (asaṃmoha) is among the states that arise from him (10.4).
antidotes: Knowledge of the imperishable embodied one (2.13, 2.30)
The brāhmī sthiti, after which one is not deluded (2.72)
the end of sin, freedom from the pairs (7.28)
knowing the Lord as unborn, without beginning, the great lord of the world (10.3)

name: Delusion (moha)
description: The worst fault, since attachment and aversion arise only in the deluded.

name: The thirty grounds of deluding karma
description: Acts so grave that they bind the strongest deluding karma — killing beings cruelly, betraying a teacher or the community, falsely claiming to be a monk or omniscient, and others — listed in the ninth chapter of the Daśāśrutaskandha.

name: The fetters of death (mṛtyu-pāśa)
description: Death's fetters, from which the long-life rites lift a person 'with divine speech'; the Tryambaka verse asks release from death, not from immortality.

name: Attachment (mūrcchā)
description: Infatuation with what one has — the inner essence of possessiveness ('possession is attachment'); one who gives up the thought 'mine' gives up what is his.

name: The ten offences against the name
description: Blaspheming devotees; regarding Śiva's names and qualities as independent of Viṣṇu's; disregarding the guru; deriding scripture; taking the name's glories as exaggeration; interpreting the name fancifully; sinning on its strength; equating it with other pious acts; teaching it to the faithless; lacking love for it despite hearing its glories (clinging to 'I and mine'); inattention is often added.

name: Unbelief (nāstikya) and the 'Lokāyata' reading of Mīmāṃsā
description: Denial of the self, the afterlife and the Veda's authority; Kumārila writes to lead Mīmāṃsā, 'mostly made Lokāyata', back onto the āstika path, and presents Śabara's proof of the self as its refutation.

name: The near and far enemies of the divine abidings
description: Each divine abiding is threatened by a near enemy resembling it and a far enemy opposed to it.
members: upekkhā: unknowing equanimity (near), greed and resentment (far)

name: Nidāna (binding wish for reward)
description: Wishing that one's austerities bring worldly or heavenly reward — a thorn, a sorrowful meditation and a fault of the final fast (TS 7.37, 9.33).

name: Sleep as a bond of tamas (nidrā)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Sleep is one of the three — with heedlessness and indolence — by which tamas binds the embodied one (14.8).
